task.name: hardening: enforce per-test timeouts in gate runs
task.story_text:
CONVENTIONS.md states that every test must complete in under five seconds and
that no test may perform blocking I/O without a timeout. Nothing enforces it. The
rule is advisory prose, so a test that violates it is discovered only when it
consumes an entire gate run.

When that happens the gate's verdict carries no attribution. The suite is killed as
a whole, so the run ends without a complete verdict and without naming the test
that consumed the budget. Whatever the log happens to show before the kill — some
assertion failures, the termination line — the one thing it cannot supply is which
test was responsible, and whether it was slow or genuinely blocked.

## Why

Re-evidenced on 2026-08-29. A sprint on #2681 cycled through repeated DEV
iterations without ever establishing whether the branch's tests passed: a newly
added production wait caused pre-existing, previously-compliant coordinator tests
to block, and the suite was terminated past ten minutes with no summary. The
absence of a named culprit then produced competing reconstructions of the failure,
none of which the artifacts could settle quickly.

The bound cannot be enforced by asking developers to honour it. The tests that
blocked here were not written in violation of the rule — they were compliant when
written, and a change elsewhere in the tree made them slow. No authoring-time
discipline reaches that case; only an enforced budget does.

## Scope

Enforcing the bound exposes pre-existing tests that already violate the five-second
rule. Bringing those tests under the bound while preserving their coverage is **in
scope for this story** — they are directly related to it, and the general prohibition
on modifying existing tests unrelated to a story does not apply to them.

The first remedy is to make them faster. No test is skipped, excluded from the
default gate, or moved out of the merge path to get the suite green. Where a test's
cost is inherent to production machinery it must exercise rather than to the test's
own design, it may instead declare a category bound as described in the criteria
below; establishing that inherency is the dev's burden — say what was measured and
why the cost cannot be removed.

## Acceptance criteria

- The test configuration checked into the repository declares a per-test time bound
  matching the documented five-second rule, and whatever the runner needs in order
  to enforce it is a declared development dependency rather than an assumption
  about the environment.
- The bound is declared once, in configuration, so that every invocation of the
  suite inherits it without a flag being passed — the project gate, the developer
  check, and a bare runner invocation in a terminal alike. An invocation nobody
  anticipated inherits the bound rather than escaping it.
- A test that blocks past the bound is named in the run's output together with a
  stack trace locating where it was stuck, so the run's failure is attributable
  rather than anonymous. A deterministic test demonstrates this using its own short
  bound, so the demonstration does not add the default bound's duration to every
  run.
- The baseline suite remains green under enforcement without skips, broad
  exclusions, or widening the shared bound.
- A per-test override may shorten the bound — for example, for a deterministic test
  that proves the enforcement works.
- A test may declare a larger bound only by belonging to a narrow, named category:
  one that orchestrates real processes, real repositories, or a full sprint workflow.
  Such a test stays in the default gate and stays bounded — it declares a larger
  explicit bound, and exceeding that bound still fails with the test named and a
  stack trace. Ordinary tests may not raise the bound for any reason, and no test
  leaves the merge path.
- The set of tests carrying a raised bound is explicit and enumerable in one place,
  and cannot grow without a deliberate, visible change to that enumeration.
  Acquiring a raised bound is never a side effect of making a test pass.

## Example

Today, a coordinator test that blocks on a real polling path ends the run like this
— no test name, no stack trace, no exit status:

```
........................................F...............   [ 91%]
make: *** [dev-check] Terminated: 15
```

Afterwards the same test should be named as having exceeded the bound, with a stack
trace showing where it was stuck, so the failure is attributable to it rather than
to the run as a whole.

## Observed on the two failed attempts (measured 2026-08-30)

Both dev iterations implemented the bound and both deadlocked the suite. Direct
measurements on an idle machine:

- Base branch `make gate`: **92s** wall clock, 10,296 passed, 0 failed.
- With enforcement configured as `timeout = 5` / `timeout_method = "signal"` under
  `[tool.pytest.ini_options]`, alongside the pre-existing
  `addopts = "-n auto --dist worksteal"`: the run reaches ~99%, stops, and never
  finishes — still running past **600s**, versus 92s green on base.
- At that point all ten xdist workers are alive at **0.0% CPU**. Sampling one shows
  its main thread parked acquiring a lock, and its execnet receiver thread blocked
  reading from the master:

```
main-thread
  ... method_vectorcall_VARARGS_KEYWORDS
        lock_PyThread_acquire_lock
          acquire_timed
            PyThread_acquire_lock_timed      <-- parked here indefinitely

receiver thread
  _io__Buffered_read -> _bufferedreader_raw_read -> _io_FileIO_readinto
    -> _Py_read -> read
```

Zero CPU across every worker distinguishes this from a slow suite: nothing is
executing, and nothing will wake up. The gate reports only
`TIMEOUT after 360s: make gate`, so neither iteration was ever shown this.

Related hazard already recorded in CONVENTIONS.md: forked xdist workers that inherit
a held lock deadlock. This is evidence of what happens, not a prescription for which
enforcement mechanism to use.

conventions_soft[0].value: Coordinator is pure Python — no LLM calls for routing or process decisions

conventions_soft[1].value: Schema validation is the integrity boundary — do not relax cross-validation rules

conventions_soft[2].value: Keep modules single-purpose. Extract when a responsibility separates from its neighbours — never to satisfy a line count. Putting a change in an already-large module is correct if that is where it belongs; a module carved at whatever line got the count down is worse than the large module it came from.

conventions_soft[3].value: Keep pure-data types in low-dependency modules with stdlib-only imports

conventions_soft[4].value: Separate prompt construction, output parsing, and coordinator control flow

conventions_soft[5].value: When adding or modifying data that flows between coordinator phases, instrument the change so the actual values are visible in the audit trail — diagnosing sprint failures requires tracing real data, not reconstructing it

conventions_soft[6].value: Do not create files outside src/, tests/, or docs/. If you need a scratch file for exploration, delete it before committing.

conventions_soft[7].value: Changes that affect coordinator phase boundaries, state handoff between phases, or adaptive routing/config propagation must include seam-level integration tests covering the touched boundary. Unit tests alone are insufficient when correctness depends on cross-phase state flow.

handoff.summary: The amended spec's category criteria resolved the impasse that ten prior cycles of measurement had established, and the suite now runs with zero timeouts. Raising the bound requires two deliberate steps and one is not enough: the test carries @pytest.mark.orchestration and its nodeid is listed in tests/timeout_enforcement.py::ORCHESTRATION_BOUND_TESTS. Either alone grants nothing, which is the direct answer to 'acquiring a raised bound is never a side effect' — adding a marker is not enough, and editing the list is not enough. The enumeration is the single place the set lives, and a test guards it both ways: every entry must name a test that still exists, catching rot after a rename, and no collected test may carry the marker without being listed, catching the side-effect path. These six tests stay in the default gate and stay bounded, each declaring its own value from 10s to 20s sized against its measured serial time, under a 30s category ceiling; exceeding a declared bound still fails with the test named and a stack trace, and disabling or reshaping enforcement is still rejected inside the category. Each entry records its measurement and what was tried and rejected on evidence rather than assumption: splitting (every assertion group reads state one sprint produced, so a split runs the sprint twice, and func_only=False means a module-scoped fixture is still charged to the first test requesting it), removing the remote publish (it is what prunes staging, so stubbing it made a test 3.5x slower at 1.77s to 6.22s), fewer runs in the adaptive test (it asserts the promotion floor itself), and three candidate hot spots each measured away — lease sweep 8%, gh 0.03s, tracker thread creation 0.02ms under 500 extra processes. Worth flagging: my first version of the enumeration guard spawned --collect-only over 10,000 tests and timed out on its first run, which is exactly the failure this story enforces against; I rewrote it to record the marked set during the collection already happening, so the check is free.

acceptance_criteria.notes: validate_timeout_mark accepts shorter numeric overrides positionally and by keyword, and the xdist demonstration uses @pytest.mark.timeout(0.25). Rejects timeout(0), negative values, method=/timeout_method= (keyword and positional), func_only=True, and non-numeric or bool values without crashing collection. Marks are read via iter_markers so module-level pytestmark and parametrized marks are covered.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: A test may declare a larger bound only by belonging to a narrow, named category: one that orchestrates real processes, real repositories, or a full sprint workflow. Such a test stays in the default gate and stays bounded — it declares a larger explicit bound, and exceeding that bound still fails with the test named and a stack trace. Ordinary tests may not raise the bound for any reason, and no test leaves the merge path.
acceptance_criteria.notes: The category is @pytest.mark.orchestration, registered in pyproject markers with its meaning and the fact that the marker alone grants nothing. Six tests carry it, each declaring an explicit @pytest.mark.timeout of 10-20s sized against its measured serial time, under ORCHESTRATION_MAX_SECONDS = 30.0. Nothing is skipped, deselected or moved off the default gate — all six run in the normal suite. Exceeding a declared bound fails through the same pytest-timeout path with the culprit named and its stack re-emitted. test_an_ordinary_test_still_cannot_raise_the_bound proves an unmarked, unlisted test is still rejected at 20s, and that the rejection message names both the marker and the enumeration so the next person is pointed at the sanctioned route rather than a workaround. test_the_category_raises_the_bound_but_does_not_remove_it proves the ceiling holds and that timeout(0) is still rejected inside the category.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: The set of tests carrying a raised bound is explicit and enumerable in one place, and cannot grow without a deliberate, visible change to that enumeration. Acquiring a raised bound is never a side effect of making a test pass.
acceptance_criteria.notes: ORCHESTRATION_BOUND_TESTS in tests/timeout_enforcement.py is the one place, a literal frozenset of nodeids with each entry's measurement in a comment. raised_bound_allowed requires BOTH the marker and membership, so neither editing the list nor adding the marker grants anything alone — proven by test_the_category_needs_both_the_marker_and_the_enumeration, which checks a listed-but-unmarked item and a marked-but-unlisted item are both refused. test_the_enumeration_cannot_rot_or_grow_unnoticed guards both directions: entries must name tests that still exist (catching a rename), and no collected test may carry the marker without being listed (catching the side-effect path). That check reads the marked set recorded during the collection already in progress, so it costs nothing.

story_deviations: The category ceiling (ORCHESTRATION_MAX_SECONDS = 30.0) is mine rather than the spec's; the criterion requires the category to stay bounded but names no cap. Without one the category would be an open-ended escape hatch, which is the failure mode the enumeration exists to prevent. 30s is generous against the contention measured on these tests (a 1.06s test reaching 5s, a 4.7x inflation) and far below the 600s hang the story is about.

Existing test files were modified under the Scope section's authorisation across cycles: test_issue_body_producer_conformance.py, test_no_test_double_detection_guard.py, test_process_group.py, test_sandbox_group_kill.py, test_sprint_terminal_lifecycle.py, test_sprint_parallel.py, test_process_tree.py, test_protected_base_publication_poc.py, test_coord_adaptive_assignment_runtime.py, test_sprint_run_artifact_publish_timing.py. No assertion was removed or weakened anywhere; the drain-window change strengthened one, verified by mutation.

Four production files were changed in earlier cycles, each because a hard-coded timing or repeated-work choice was what put tests over the bound, and each preserving behaviour and defaults: process_group.py resolves three grace defaults through a `_grace` helper at call time; sprint/runner.py names the scheduling tick PLAN_GATE_TICK_SECONDS at the same value; cli/shared.py renders the run audit once per content state rather than once per copy. Nothing in process_group/process_tree containment scanning was touched after the operator's instruction.
deferred_items: FINDING, worth its own story: forge's per-spawn process supervision costs 4.11ms on top of the command itself (bare `git --version` 3.51ms, through _run_shell 7.82ms) and grows with the host process table (5.93ms idle, 9.89ms with 200 extra processes) while plain subprocess cost stays flat. Source is util.py:560-592 — register_agent_group, descendant_tracker(...).start(), and the release-time lease sweep. The process-table scan measures 1.6ms and thread creation ~0ms, so scans are the largest single component at roughly half the total, with the rest in sidecar write, lease sweep and fork/exec bookkeeping. Do not chase thread creation. Reducing this would let several enumerated tests drop back to the shared bound.

FINDING, worth its own story: a memory publish that has nothing to commit costs 12-14 subprocess spawns to discover it, reaching the 'Everything staged is already on the memory branch' branch at memory_publication.py:414-420 only after git fetch, git worktree add, a copy, git add --force and an empty git status — 26 spawns and 346ms over a two-story sprint. It accumulates because staging retains content until the base branch absorbs it. A sound in-process memo is available (skip the worktree when the resolved start-point sha and the staged files' content hashes are both unchanged since the last CLEAN verdict), avoiding the mode and filter subtleties of comparing against git blobs directly.

METHOD NOTE for future timeout diagnosis: a dump's stack is the frame executing when the timer fires, so for a test making 100-200 supervised spawns it is a time-weighted sample, not a hot spot. Across this story the dumps landed at six different frames inside the same publish path, none reproducing. Treat a repeated frame as a lead; treat scatter as evidence the cost is spread.

Tests racing a fixed window rather than exceeding a budget remain a distinct fragility class worth a sweep: test_records_a_grandchild_that_left_the_group ran in 0.08s serially and still failed the gate because its 2s parent-link hold closed under load. That instance is fixed. test_a_story_refused_before_integration_does_not_refuse_its_siblings holds a story open on a 60s Event wait, which would blow its bound outright if the story it waits for were ever not dispatched.

soft: Coordinator is pure Python — no LLM calls for routing or process decisions
Schema validation is the integrity boundary — do not relax cross-validation rules

Keep modules single-purpose. Extract when a responsibility separates from its neighbours — never to satisfy a line count. Putting a change in an already-large module is correct if that is where it belongs; a module carved at whatever line got the count down is worse than the large module it came from.
Keep pure-data types in low-dependency modules with stdlib-only imports
Separate prompt construction, output parsing, and coordinator control flow

When adding or modifying data that flows between coordinator phases, instrument the change so the actual values are visible in the audit trail — diagnosing sprint failures requires tracing real data, not reconstructing it
Do not create files outside src/, tests/, or docs/. If you need a scratch file for exploration, delete it before committing.

Changes that affect coordinator phase boundaries, state handoff between phases, or adaptive routing/config propagation must include seam-level integration tests covering the touched boundary. Unit tests alone are insufficient when correctness depends on cross-phase state flow.
